scope: Independent recognition of ORIGINAL preserved audio; errors and numbers need human listening; never perceptual approval

segments.text: A family is planning a trip to the wildlife park. Three buses leave at different times, which one arrives before the gates open.
Today we are learning to read time tables and calculate travel durations.
Our learning goal is to read time tables and calculate travel duration.
Success criteria, read the part-time, calculate elapsed time and choose a suitable journey.
Read the departure and arrival times from the same service on the timetable. Different rows can refer to different journeys.
A timeline makes the journey visible. Begin at 8.25, move to 9.00 and then move to 9.10.
How many minutes pass between 825 and 910?
35 minutes to 9, a clock plus 10 minutes to 9, 10, makes 45 minutes.
24-hour time removes confusion between morning and afternoon. 13-15 means 1-15 in the afternoon.
A train departs at 1315 and arrives at 1405. How long is the journey?
45 minutes to 14 hundred and five more minutes. The journey lasts 50 minutes.
Subtracting the minute numbers alone is a mistake when you cross an hour. Use the full timeline instead.
For a deadline, consider arrival time, not just departure time. Arriving after an event begins, maybe too late.
You must arrive before 10. A service arrives at 935. Does it meet the deadline?
Yes 935 is 25 minutes before 10 so the service meets the deadline.
Remember to include walking and waiting time. Reaching the station exactly when the bus leaves is risky.
A bus departs at 920 and arrives at 10.05. How many minutes does the trip take?
40 minutes to 10 o'clock then 5 more minutes. The trip lasts 45 minutes.
Check that your answer is sensible. A journey crossing an hour can be longer than the difference between the minute digits.
A train leaves at 1135 and arrives at 1220. Calculate the duration using noon.
25 minutes to noon plus 20 minutes afterwards makes 45 minutes.
Read the correct time table entry. Draw a timeline. Cross the hour boundary and add the intervals.
Think about a school bus timetable. The departure time tells us when to be at the stop while the arrival time tells us when we can reach our destination.
If the bus is delayed, our original plan may no longer work. A good traveler checks whether there is enough time before an important appointment.
Try a different strategy. Instead of counting every minute, split the journey at the nearest whole hour and add the two intervals.
A journey from 935 to 10 o'clock takes 25 minutes. We know this because 60 minus 35 equals 25.
Check your answer by counting forward. Start at 935 at 25 minutes and you should reach 10 o'clock.
If you have to change buses, calculate the waiting time between the first arrival and the second departure. That way is part of the whole trip.
A timetable is a promise about plan times but it is not the same as a clock. We use the timetable to predict when the journey should happen.
Suppose you need 10 minutes to walk from the bus stop to the wildlife park. A bus arriving at 955 would not get you through the gate by 10.
When comparing two routes, the shortest ride is not always the earliest arrival. A little departure may still arrive sooner if it travels more directly.
Imagine a service that leaves at 840 and arrives at 920. Count 20 minutes to 9, then 20 more to 920.
A transfer means leaving one service and boarding another. Calculate the gap between the first arrival and the second departure before choosing the route.
If your connection arrives at 9/10 and the next bus leaves at 9/12, you have only 2 minutes to change. Is that a sensible plan?
The answer depends on how far apart the platforms are. Good planning includes a safety margin, not only the arithmetic.
Now create a small timetable with two departure options, give each and arrival time and decide which service is better for a morning appointment.
estimate before you calculate a journey from 1135 to 1220 must be shorter than an hour because 1235 would be one hour later.
You can explain your thinking with words, numbers or a timeline. The strongest answer shows where each interval comes from.
